about: A word list for IRL streaming, one entry per term. Fields: id (an anchor), term, also_called (true synonyms), search_terms (search only), aliases (deprecated, generated from the fields before it), tier (core | more), who (streamer | helper | both), heard_when, plain, related (ids), source, uncertain, optional l10n: {<language tag>: {term, plain, heard_when}} such as es-419 or pt-BR, and optional naming: a naming guide for app makers (recommended label, other names with a status, dated evidence). Translations keep the scene's English terms as the term and explain in the language, and are read by a native speaker before publishing. Validated by the zod schema in ../schema.

words.heard_when: Streamers talk about going live away from their desk, whether that's in the kitchen, at a venue or on the street.
words.plain: Short for "in real life". It means streaming your real life away from your desk or gaming setup: in the kitchen at home, at a venue, outside or on the move.

words.heard_when: A phone isn't enough any more and someone suggests a bag with modems.
words.plain: A bag with a small computer, a big battery and several mobile internet connections inside. It turns your camera's picture into a live stream.

words.heard_when: Setting up a second network, or choosing an app or backpack.
words.plain: Using several internet connections at the same time for one stream, like two phones' data and Wi-Fi. If one gets weak, the others keep it going.

naming.label: Bonding
naming.scope: A switch, status or section about sending one stream over several connections at the same time.
naming.why: One short word that people already search for and say in chat. It names what happens, not the protocol, so it still fits when an app offers more than one way to bond.

alternatives.why: The networking term the SRTLA protocol is named after. Accurate, but most streamers don't use it.
One protocol for bonding. Useful where an app offers a choice of protocols.
The group of connections in use, rather than the act of combining them. Works for a status such as "in the bond".

evidence.note: Toggle labelled "Bonding" in the RIST stream settings.
evidence.label: Bonding

evidence.note: "Use for bonding" on a network link; the same catalogue has "Bonded Links" and "Enable Bond".
evidence.label: Use for bonding

evidence.note: "Use for bonding" on a network link; the same catalogue has "Bonded Links" and "Enable Bond".
evidence.label: Bonded Links

evidence.note: "Use for bonding" on a network link; the same catalogue has "Bonded Links" and "Enable Bond".
evidence.label: Enable Bond

evidence.note: Feature list on the app's page: "SRTLA Bonding over multiple connections". A feature name, not a settings screen.
evidence.label: SRTLA Bonding over multiple connections

naming.translation_note: If your language has no settled word, keep "bonding" and explain it once in a hint. Don't translate it as a word for glue or ties.

words.heard_when: When you set up bonding, or read the guide for a relay service or your own receiver
words.plain: A computer on the internet that collects your stream's pieces from every connection. It joins them back into one stream for OBS or the platform.

naming.label: Relay server
naming.scope: Where the sender picks the server that collects a bonded stream and passes it on to OBS or the platform.
naming.why: "Server" makes clear that this is a computer on the internet. On its own, "relay" can also mean a phone that lends its connection.

alternatives.why: The same thing, named from the receiving side. Common for a receiver you run yourself.
Names the protocol. Useful next to the address and port fields.
In some apps a relay is a second phone or device that adds its connection to the stream, not a server.

evidence.note: Field labels "Relay server" and "SRTLA receiver address" in the relay settings.
evidence.label: Relay server

evidence.note: Field labels "Relay server" and "SRTLA receiver address" in the relay settings.
evidence.label: SRTLA receiver address

evidence.note: "Relay Server" (title case); the server dialog is titled "Receiver Server".
evidence.label: Relay Server

evidence.note: "Relay Server" (title case); the server dialog is titled "Receiver Server".
evidence.label: Receiver Server

evidence.note: Section "Relay" for the device that adds an extra bonding connection, not a server.
evidence.label: Relay

naming.translation_note: Translate "server"; "relay" can stay in English if the local word sounds like an electrical relay.

words.heard_when: Output settings in Moblin, Larix or BELABOX; an srt:// address from a relay or cloud OBS; OBS Media Source receiving SRT
words.plain: A way of sending live video over the internet. When a piece gets lost on the way, it is sent again quickly, so the picture glitches less.

words.heard_when: Bonding settings in BELABOX and Moblin; a relay or receiver service gives you an SRTLA host and port
words.plain: A way of splitting one live video across several internet connections at once. A computer at the other end joins the pieces up again.

words.heard_when: OBS output settings; backpacks and apps described as encoders
words.plain: The app or box that shrinks your camera's picture and sound so they fit through an internet connection. It works a bit like zipping a big file before sending it.

words.heard_when: Relay and hosting services that include OBS; IRL setups with nothing running at home
words.plain: OBS, the free program that builds what viewers see, running on a rented computer in a data centre. Nothing at home has to stay switched on.

words.heard_when: 'Switch to BRB'; stepping away for a moment; the stream jumping to a BRB screen when the signal drops
words.plain: Short for "be right back". It's the screen viewers see while you take a break or your signal is gone.

naming.label: BRB scene
naming.scope: The scene or screen shown while the streamer is away or the signal is gone, where an app lets you pick it.
naming.why: "Scene" tells the reader they pick one of their own scenes. BRB alone is fine where space is short.

alternatives.why: The words BRB stands for. Clearer to newcomers, but long for a label.

evidence.note: "BRB scene" in the OBS remote control settings, and a toggle "BRB scene when video source is broken".
evidence.label: BRB scene

evidence.note: "BRB scene" in the OBS remote control settings, and a toggle "BRB scene when video source is broken".
evidence.label: BRB scene when video source is broken

naming.translation_note: Keep BRB as written; it's chat shorthand. A translated name can follow it in a hint.

words.heard_when: Choosing cloud production or a hosted relay; NOALBS switching to a BRB scene when the feed drops
words.plain: Your setup switches to your BRB scene when the connection drops, then back when it returns. There is no time limit.

naming.label: Drop protection
naming.scope: Automatic switching to your own BRB scene and back in your production setup, without a time limit.
naming.why: Names the whole feature in two words, and "drop" is what streamers call losing the signal.

alternatives.why: Moblin uses the same name as Twitch's platform feature.
The scene it switches to, not the whole feature.
The picture it switches to, not the whole feature.
The scene shown while the feed is gone, not the switching itself.

evidence.note: The product page lists "drop protection" and "Drop protection with NOALBS" as plan features. A feature name, not a settings screen.
evidence.label: drop protection

evidence.note: The product page lists "drop protection" and "Drop protection with NOALBS" as plan features. A feature name, not a settings screen.
evidence.label: Drop protection with NOALBS

evidence.note: Settings page "Disconnect protection" with a picker "Fallback scene".
evidence.label: Disconnect protection

evidence.note: Settings page "Disconnect protection" with a picker "Fallback scene".
evidence.label: Fallback scene

evidence.note: The NoDrop guide names the setting "Fallback Source".
evidence.label: Fallback Source

evidence.note: The config calls the scene used when the feed is gone the "offline" scene.
evidence.label: offline

evidence.note: Behind-login feature text supplied on 16 November 2026 uses this label for cloud production; it does not specify BRB return behaviour or a time limit. URL: public login page.
evidence.label: disconnection protection

naming.translation_note: Translate the meaning (protection when the connection drops), not the word "drop" literally.

words.heard_when: Turning on Twitch's backup screen for a lost connection
words.plain: Twitch keeps your broadcast open for up to 90 seconds when your connection drops, showing its own waiting screen. If you do not return, the broadcast ends.

naming.label: Disconnect protection
naming.scope: The platform holds a broadcast open briefly after the incoming connection drops.
naming.why: Twitch's name for its platform-side hold.

alternatives.why: The streamer’s own setup switches scenes rather than the platform holding the broadcast open.

evidence.label: Disconnect Protection
evidence.note: Twitch describes its Disconnect Protection feature: viewers see a BRB screen for up to 90 seconds while the mobile streamer reconnects.

naming.translation_note: Keep the distinction between the platform hold and switching scenes in the streamer’s own setup.

words.heard_when: Mobile plan terms, carrier texts when you near the limit, 'unlimited' plans that still have limits
words.plain: How much mobile data your phone plan includes. Using more can cost extra. One hour of a typical stream (6 megabits each second) uses about 2.7 GB.

words.heard_when: Speed-test apps; OBS and platform advice to keep bitrate well below it
words.plain: How fast your connection can send things out, not bring them in. Streaming is all sending, so this is the number that matters.

words.heard_when: OBS output settings, every IRL app's stats line, a relay's stats page, chat asking why the picture went blocky
words.plain: How much data your stream sends every second. More data means a sharper picture, but it needs a stronger connection.

naming.label: Bitrate
naming.scope: How much data per second the encoder aims for or may use, in kbit/s or Mbit/s.
naming.why: One word that every app checked uses in some form. Say next to it whether the value is a limit or a target, and give the unit.

alternatives.why: The upper limit when the app changes the bitrate by itself.
Only the picture. Use it where an audio bitrate sits next to it.

evidence.note: Slider value shown as "Max bitrate: … Kbps".
evidence.label: Max bitrate

evidence.note: "Bitrate (Kbps)" in the encoder dialog; "Max bitrate" on the go-live card.
evidence.label: Bitrate (Kbps)

evidence.note: "Bitrate (Kbps)" in the encoder dialog; "Max bitrate" on the go-live card.
evidence.label: Max bitrate

evidence.note: Picker labelled "Bitrate" in the video settings of a stream.
evidence.label: Bitrate

evidence.note: The knowledge base names the setting "Video Bitrate" under Settings → Output.
evidence.label: Video Bitrate

naming.translation_note: Many languages keep "bitrate" as a loanword. Keep the unit as kbit/s or Mbit/s; don't translate it.

words.heard_when: Moblin and IRL Pro bitrate settings; OBS Advanced → Network 'dynamically change bitrate'; bonding encoders
words.plain: The app makes the picture a bit blurrier by itself when your connection gets weak, so the stream keeps going. It sharpens again when the signal improves.

words.heard_when: Stats in BELABOX, Moblin, relays and SRT receivers; 'the link is fine but loss is high'; often confused with OBS's dropped frames
words.plain: Little pieces of your stream that go missing on the way. A few can be sent again in time; too many cause glitches or a drop.

words.heard_when: The latency setting in BELABOX, Moblin, IRL Pro and relays, in milliseconds; 'raise the latency on bad networks'
words.plain: How long the receiving end waits for late or missing pieces before showing the picture. Waiting longer means fewer glitches, but viewers see things later.

naming.label: SRT latency
naming.scope: The receive buffer of an SRT or SRTLA connection, set in milliseconds.
naming.why: Naming the protocol keeps it apart from the delay viewers see. Show the unit (ms) next to the value.

alternatives.why: Also means the whole delay from camera to viewer. Clear enough only inside a section that is already about SRT.
What the setting is underneath. Good in a hint, less familiar as a label.
Describes the mechanism. Fine in a hint.
Many settings are buffers: audio, jitter, recording.

evidence.note: Slider value shown as "SRT latency: … ms".
evidence.label: SRT latency

evidence.note: "Latency" inside the SRT settings of a stream, shown in ms.
evidence.label: Latency

evidence.note: "Latency" in the latency section of the server dialog.
evidence.label: Latency

naming.translation_note: Keep "SRT" as written. Translate "latency" with the word your language uses for delay in network settings.

words.heard_when: YouTube's latency choice, Twitch's low-latency option, chat answering a moment late
words.plain: The time between something happening in front of your camera and viewers seeing it. Shorter feels more live, but the video can stop to load more often.

words.heard_when: OBS Scenes dock, Moblin's scene buttons, a helper saying 'switch to BRB' or 'go to the starting scene'
words.plain: One saved layout of what viewers see, such as your camera, a break screen or "starting soon". Switching changes the whole picture at once.

words.heard_when: Moblin's SRT settings; a bond that works on one network but not over an Android phone's hotspot
words.plain: A Moblin setting that puts slightly more video into each little piece it sends. It's on by default; Moblin says some Android phone hotspots don't work with it.

words.heard_when: Moblin's SRT settings; a connection that connects but sends nothing on one mobile network
words.plain: A Moblin setting for how the app looks up the internet address of the computer it sends to. On some networks, another choice connects better.

words.heard_when: iPhone Settings → Personal Hotspot; connecting a camera to a phone's hotspot
words.plain: An iPhone hotspot setting that switches to an older Wi-Fi band, so older devices can join. Apple says it can lower performance.

words.heard_when: Moblin scene settings with all settings shown; the sound jumping to another mic after a scene change
words.plain: A Moblin setting that ties one microphone to one screen layout. When that layout comes on, the sound switches to that mic.

words.heard_when: OBS Sources → Browser; adding alerts, chat or a map from a web address
words.plain: A part of an OBS layout that shows a web page, like alerts, chat or a map. If it's hidden, it may not play at all.

words.heard_when: Feeding a camera into Moblin, MediaSrvr or a backpack over Wi-Fi
words.plain: A small receiving point inside your app or box. A camera sends its picture to it over Wi-Fi or a cable, so the app can use it.

words.heard_when: Setting up OBS for IRL; 'use NOALBS for your BRB'
words.plain: A free tool that watches how much video is arriving. It switches OBS to your low-signal or break screen by itself, and back again.

words.heard_when: Encoder advanced settings; a platform's recommended settings list
words.plain: Some frames in a video are saved as only the changes from the frames before and after them. That saves data. Streaming sites say how many to use.

words.heard_when: Cloud OBS and relay dashboards; the app says live but the platform says offline
words.plain: With an online streaming service, your stream arrives there first. Then the service sends it on to Twitch or YouTube. You have to start each half separately.

words.heard_when: Scene switcher settings; a bitrate overlay; OBS has video but the switcher shows nothing
words.plain: A web address where the receiving computer shows how much video is coming in. Switching tools read it. It isn't where the picture itself comes from.

words.heard_when: Scene switcher settings; good bitrate but the switcher keeps going to BRB
words.plain: A switching tool's setting that names the software on your receiving computer. Each program reports its numbers differently.

words.heard_when: NOALBS's Live page and chat commands; back on LIVE but the picture is frozen
words.plain: A NOALBS button and chat command (!fix) that reconnects the video in what viewers are watching right now.

words.heard_when: App settings labelled 'video codec'; a platform's list of the formats it accepts
words.plain: The method used to shrink video so it fits through the internet. Your app and the platform must both handle the same one.
